questions.q: A country has a comparative advantage in a good if it can produce it:
questions.why: Producing more from the same resources is absolute advantage.

questions.q: A worker can make {x} phones or {y} shirts. What is the opportunity cost of 1 phone, in shirts?
Country A is better at making both of two goods. Can trade still help both countries?
options: Yes, if their opportunity costs differ
Only if they share a currency
questions.why: Comparative advantage, not absolute advantage, is what matters.

questions.q: The simple model of comparative advantage ignores transport costs.
questions.why: Real trade has transport costs and barriers.

questions.q: Which best describes the UK's trade pattern?
options: A deficit in goods and a surplus in services
A surplus in goods and a deficit in services
questions.why: The UK specialises heavily in services such as finance.

questions.q: Explain how free trade can benefit consumers.

ideas.label: More competition or specialisation lowers costs and prices
Consumers get more choice or better quality, or real incomes rise

questions.model: Competition from abroad lowers prices, so real incomes rise. Consumers also get more choice and better quality.

tests.answer: Competition lowers prices and gives more choice.
